content: Carbon suboxide, also known as tricarbon dioxide and represented by the chemical formula C3O2, is a colorless gas with a strong, pungent odor. Its molecular structure contains four consecutive double bonds, classifying it as a cumulene. This compound is chemically related to other carbon oxides, such as carbon monoxide (CO), carbon dioxide (CO2), and dicarbon monoxide (C2O). The compound was first discovered in 1873 by Brodie, who generated it by passing an electric current through carbon monoxide. The name carbon suboxide was later introduced by Marcellin Berthelot, although Otto Diels suggested that alternative names like dicarbonyl methane and dioxallene were also appropriate. Carbon suboxide can be synthesized by heating a dry mixture of phosphorus pentoxide (P4O10) and malonic acid or its esters. This synthesis method highlights its relationship to malonic acid, as it can be considered the second anhydride of malonic acid, or the anhydride of malonic anhydride. It is important to note that malonic anhydride is a distinct and real chemical entity, not to be confused with maleic anhydride. Additional methods for synthesizing and studying the reactions of carbon suboxide were detailed in a 1930 review by Reyerson. One notable property of carbon suboxide is its tendency to polymerize spontaneously, forming solid materials that can appear red, yellow, or black. The polymerized structure is believed to resemble poly(α-pyronic), which is similar to the structure of 2-pyrone (α-pyrone). In 1969, it was hypothesized that the reddish coloration of the Martian surface might be due to the presence of carbon suboxide. However, this theory was later disproven following data obtained from the Viking mission to Mars.
